newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: France takes centre stage at EU fin mins meeting.
newsitem.headline: France takes centre stage at EU fin mins meeting.

text.p: France was set to take centre stage on Monday at a European Union finance ministers meeting likely to be dominated by concerns over the new French government's views on aspects of the single currency.

Ministers emerged from a dinner on Sunday evening saying they had been reassured by new French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn that Paris was still firmly committed to economic and monetary union (EMU) on January 1, 1999.

"It's quite clear that the French government is in favour of the EMU process and respecting the treaty of Maastricht," Dutch Finance Minster Gerrit Zalm, whose country is EU president, said after Sunday's dinner.
"Mr Strauss-Kahn let us know that the January 1, 1999 date will be respected," Luxembourg Finance and Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker added.
Strauss-Kahn himself said he did not know why anyone would have doubted the commitment.

But the ministers left until Monday one of the key questions that has arisen since French Socialists won a stunning election victory last week -- the stability pact agreed in December but due to be ratified formally at a summit in Amsterdam next week.
French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who has pledged to fight austerity in Europe, said during the election campaign he did not feel bound by the pact.

Ministers were quick to say, however, that they had been reassured that there could be a way to assuage France's fears about the pact without reopening negotiations, which would trigger a crisis with Germany, which sees it as a guarantee of fiscal discipline after the launch of the euro in 1999.
"We can find the ways and means to reach an agreement in Amsterdam," Juncker said.

After two weeks of turmoil triggered by the French elections and Germany's plans to revalue its gold reserves -- seen as an accounting ploy to help Bonn qualify for EMU -- the ministers also sought to dismiss talk of a delay in the currency's launch.
"The clear underlying message (from Sunday's meeting) was that EMU was on target," Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn said. "The momentum towards a single currency was being maintained."
At Monday's meeting, the ministers were first to spend two hours discussing the European Investment Bank (EIB), the EU's main lending institution.

EMU issues were expected to be discussed over lunch. As well as the stabillity pact, the ministers must endorse final rules for the legal framework of the euro and for a post-EMU exhcnage rate mechanism.
All three reports are due to be ratified in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
On Sunday night, they approved in principle various designs and technical specifications for euro coins.
Monday's focus was also expected to be on German Finance Minister Theo Waigel whose idea of revaluing gold reserves to shore up Germany's flagging finances triggered a furore.
The move raised questions about Germany's ability to meet the strict tests of EMU without resorting to creative accounting, something Bonn had sharply criticised others for attempting.
A compromise has been reached between Waigel and the Bundesbank, which vehemently opposed the plan, but Germany's difficulty in meeting EMU criteria has been given a clear public viewing.
